vopros: Who is behind Business Intelligence DNA (businessinteldna.com), and is it a legitimate company?

vyzhimka.tekst:
I looked into Business Intelligence DNA and the entity behind businessinteldna.com. It appears to be a very new business with a real identifiable legal entity behind it, but it has almost no independent operating history under the “Business Intelligence DNA” name yet. I would therefore distinguish “legally identifiable” from “established and independently validated.”

The website identifies the operator as Wealthboosterpro LLC, doing business as “Business Intelligence DNA,” with an address at 5830 E 2nd St Ste 7000, Casper, Wyoming. Its terms explicitly name two people doing the substantive client work: Andrii Zhyla, responsible for strategy/positioning, and Maryna Zhyla, described as a former CFO handling business economics. ([businessinteldna.com](https://businessinteldna.com/terms))

There is some independent evidence connecting Maryna Zhyla to the underlying business. Her LinkedIn profile lists her as working with Wealthboosterpro Corp. and describes her as an entrepreneur in the Los Angeles area. ([linkedin.com](https://www.linkedin.com/in/marinazhyla?utm_source=openai)) I did not find similarly strong independent public documentation tying Andrii Zhyla to Business Intelligence DNA, beyond the company's own terms.

One important detail: the Casper address should not be interpreted as their actual office. Wyoming's own records show 5830 E 2nd St Ste 7000 is the address of Republic Registered Agent LLC, a commercial registered agent. Many unrelated LLCs use this same address. ([sos.wyo.gov](https://sos.wyo.gov/Business/Docs/CRA-Roster.pdf?TB_iframe=true&utm_source=openai)) So the Wyoming address is consistent with a legitimate Wyoming LLC structure, but it doesn't demonstrate that the people running the business are physically based there.

There is also a notable age issue. The website's current terms only took effect on September 14, 2026, with an earlier version dating to September 8. ([businessinteldna.com](https://businessinteldna.com/terms)) More significantly, I found businessinteldna.com in a list of newly registered .com domains from September 6, 2026. ([com.all-url.info](https://com.all-url.info/21/25/?utm_source=openai)) Given that today is September 18, 2026, the Business Intelligence DNA website/brand appears to be roughly two weeks old.

That explains why searches produce virtually no independent reviews, press coverage, customer discussions, or established reputation specifically for Business Intelligence DNA. I also didn't find evidence in my searches of scam reports or complaints about the domain. Absence of complaints isn't particularly meaningful for something this new, however.

The site itself has several characteristics I'd consider positive. It clearly identifies the contracting entity and individuals providing the core service, publishes fairly detailed terms, privacy/NDA/contact documents, states its prices, and says card payments are processed through Stripe. Its advertised services currently include a $500 diagnostic engagement, implementations starting at $5,000, and AI voice-agent products starting at $1,000 plus monthly fees. ([businessinteldna.com](https://businessinteldna.com/terms)) Those are substantially more transparent disclosures than you'd typically see on an anonymous lead-generation/scam site.

There are nevertheless some reasons for caution before paying $5,000+:

- The Business Intelligence DNA brand/domain is extremely new, so there's essentially no independent track record to evaluate.
- The listed Wyoming address is a registered-agent address, not evidence of a staffed office. ([sos.wyo.gov](https://sos.wyo.gov/Business/Docs/CRA-Roster.pdf?TB_iframe=true&utm_source=openai))
- Most information about the business, its methodology, and Andrii Zhyla currently comes from the business itself rather than independent sources.
- The contract becomes relatively restrictive once work begins. For diagnostics, its terms generally say there is no refund once they receive your completed questionnaire and begin creating the work, subject to exceptions such as their failure to deliver on time. Liability is also contractually limited. ([businessinteldna.com](https://businessinteldna.com/terms))

My assessment: I don't see evidence that Business Intelligence DNA is an outright fake company or obvious scam. There are meaningful legitimacy signals, particularly the disclosed legal entity, named operators, detailed contractual terms, and an independently identifiable person associated with Wealthboosterpro. But I also wouldn't describe Business Intelligence DNA itself as an established or independently proven consultancy yet. It is apparently a brand-new offering operating through an older Wealthboosterpro entity.

If you're considering hiring them—especially for the $5,000+ implementation—I can go one level deeper and investigate Wealthboosterpro LLC, Andrii Zhyla, and Maryna Zhyla separately: corporate history, previous businesses, professional credentials, lawsuits/complaints, archived websites, and whether their claimed track record can be independently verified. That would be more informative than judging the two-week-old Business Intelligence DNA brand itself.
